Candidate-conditioned history retrieval has established precedents. DIN learns a different history aggregation for each candidate; [TWIN-V2 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16357) extends target-aware retrieval to very long histories through offline clustering and cluster-aware target attention. These support retrieving relevant older interactions instead of relying exclusively on recent-window pooling, although their CTR results do not establish gains on this Amazon benchmark. [DIN paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978).

Complementarity requires more than embedding similarity. [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02130) models complementary items as both related and dissimilar, combining low-pass and mid-pass graph filters with adaptive attention. [EII-GNN (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.inffus.2024.102691) combines dynamic cross-session transitions, per-session graphs and historical-session representations. Together, these suggest preserving transition structure separately from broad semantic resemblance; neither establishes that an observed sequential edge identifies a true complementary relationship.

An applicable research hypothesis is a small candidate-conditioned residual over SASRec: each candidate queries historical item representations using separate similarity and directional-transition channels, with recency or timestamp features. Locally trained token embeddings over titles/descriptions could share statistical strength across sparse items, while training-only transition counts supply behavioral evidence. This combination is an inferred adaptation, not a verified result from the cited papers. Treat complement/substitute channels as latent predictive patterns: interaction order and text alone do not establish ownership or functional compatibility. Evaluate the residual and its text/transition components separately using the common macro validation HR@10.
